content: Dapsone is an antibiotic that is commonly used to treat acne by reducing the number and severity of acne lesions and promoting faster healing of existing pimples. It is available in topical gel form under brand names such as Aczone. How to Use: Before applying, wash your hands thoroughly. Clean the affected skin gently using a mild or soap-free cleanser, then pat dry. Apply a small amount of the gel (approximately the size of a pea) in a thin layer to the affected areas as directed by your physician. Depending on the brand, this medication is typically applied once or twice daily. Rub the gel in gently and avoid contact with the eyes. If accidental contact occurs, rinse the eyes with plenty of water and consult your doctor if irritation persists. Use the medication consistently at the same time(s) each day to achieve the best results. Do not use more than the prescribed amount or apply it more frequently than directed. Side Effects: Common side effects include skin redness, peeling, oiliness, or dryness. Serious allergic reactions are rare but may occur. Seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms of a severe allergic reaction. This is not an exhaustive list of side effects. Contact your doctor for medical advice if you experience any concerning symptoms. Precautions: Inform your doctor if you are allergic to dapsone or any other medications, as well as if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. During pregnancy, dapsone should only be used if clearly necessary. It is known to pass into breast milk, so consult your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Drug Interactions: Dapsone may interact with other medications, potentially altering their effects or increasing the risk of side effects. It is important to inform your healthcare provider of all medications and supplements you are taking to avoid harmful interactions. Some drugs may increase or decrease the levels or effects of dapsone by affecting hepatic or intestinal enzyme metabolism, particularly involving CYP3A4, CYP2C9, or CYP2E1 enzymes. Examples include antifungals (e.g., fluconazole, voriconazole), antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and other enzyme inducers or inhibitors. Co-administration with certain drugs may increase the risk of hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, or other toxicities, especially in patients with G6PD deficiency or other predisposing conditions. Special Warnings: Dapsone may cause blood dyscrasias, such as agranulocytosis, anemia, or leukopenia. Regular monitoring of blood counts is recommended. Peripheral neuropathy, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and other dermatologic reactions have been reported. Use caution in patients with hypersensitivity to sulfonamides, as cross-reactivity may occur. Prolonged use may lead to bacterial or fungal superinfections. Dapsone is classified as pregnancy category C. While generally considered safe, it should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefits outweigh the risks. Pharmacokinetics: Dapsone is widely distributed throughout the body, particularly in the liver and kidneys, with a half-life of approximately 28 hours. It is metabolized by hepatic enzymes, including CYP2E1 and CYP3A4, and primarily excreted in the urine as metabolites. Additional Notes: Dapsone gel is for external use only and should not be ingested. Patients should adhere to their prescribed regimen and consult their healthcare provider if they experience any unusual symptoms or side effects. Keep a list of all medications you are taking and share it with your doctor to ensure safe and effective treatment.
